e7317d5a28:
This chapter is about the human process around an AI system. It covers how to:

  • turn a vague ask into a card of measurable requirements;
  • size and defend a business case with numbers, including the numbers that hurt;
  • set honest expectations about a system that isn't deterministic;
  • tell the same risk to executives, legal, security and operations;
  • assign decisions with a RACI;
  • resolve stakeholders whose requirements can't all be met;
  • design a pilot and a demo that tell the truth;
  • say no;
  • write the decision down so it survives the next reorganisation.

It includes six worked stakeholder dialogues, nineteen Python examples, and two Java ports. Chapter 1 gives the card and the first ROI model. This chapter is the human process that fills the card in and defends it.
e65ed279da:
Reading time: 3.5 to 4 hours  ·  Companion code, 19 Python and 2 Java examples for this chapter: ccarp-companion/15-discovery-requirements-stakeholders/ (run bash run_all.sh; everything works offline with --mock).

Every price, volume, rate, accuracy and stakeholder opinion in the examples is an illustrative placeholder. Before a number goes into a business case, check the docs for current model pricing. Exam facts for CCAR-P (item count, domain weights) come from third-party summaries of the published blueprint, so verify them against the official exam guide.

Cross-references: chapter 1 (card, fit test, ROI), chapter 11 (sample sizes and grading), chapter 13 (risk register, human review), chapter 16 (SLAs and lifecycle).
7c4ffb1b26:
Discovery is the work of finding the few unknowns that change the architecture, and a requirement is finished only when someone could write a test that returns pass or fail for it, with a number, a segment, a baseline and an owner.

Stakeholder communication is the same facts told four ways, to the four audiences who each own a different veto (money, law, security, operations), together with a written record of what was decided, why, and what would reopen it.
773dfe14a1:
A system built on a language model fails in a particular way. The model call rarely sinks the project. Here's what does:

  • a sponsor who heard 95 percent in a demo and understood never wrong;
  • a legal review that happened a week before launch;
  • a segment that carried the highest cost of error and was never measured;
  • an owner who left and took the meaning of the requirement with them;
  • a business case that counted the minutes saved and forgot the errors added.

None of those are model problems. They're all discovery and communication problems. And they're all cheap to prevent early and very expensive to repair late.
7826eb8119:
The blueprint for Domain 6 asks you to do five things:

  • conduct structured discovery and requirements gathering;
  • communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs to technical and non-technical stakeholders;
  • manage expectations and feedback loops, including service levels;
  • document the implementation;
  • guide a solution through its lifecycle, from discovery to monitoring and iteration.

This chapter covers the first three and the human half of the fourth. Chapter 16 covers documentation, SLAs and lifecycle mechanics in depth.

The exam presents these as scenarios where the technically attractive answer is wrong, because it skips a conversation. Maybe it's the one that pins the number. Maybe it's the one that gives legal a say before the design is frozen. Or the one that says no to an unmeasurable promise. The pattern being tested is make the ask testable, make the trade-off visible, make the decision owned and recorded.
1e94426850:
Requirements engineering is older than software engineering's complaints about it. In 1986 Fred Brooks wrote in No Silver Bullet that the hardest single part of building a software system is deciding precisely what to build. Nobody, including the customer, can specify all of it in advance.

Standards grew from that problem: IEEE 830 for software requirements specifications (1984, revised 1998), and its successor family ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (check the current edition). They gave teams a vocabulary. A requirement should be necessary, unambiguous, verifiable, consistent and traceable.

The word that matters for this chapter is verifiable. A requirement that can't be verified is a wish. The whole discipline of writing requirements is converting wishes into verifiable statements.
510b7f4dab:
Agile practice pushed the same idea closer to the team. User stories came from Extreme Programming in the late 1990s and were popularised by Mike Cohn in the early 2000s. They kept requirements short and conversational, but added acceptance criteria: the concrete examples that decide whether a story is done. Behaviour-driven development turned acceptance criteria into executable examples.

Every one of these moves has the same shape. Take a sentence a human would nod at, and attach a check a machine could run.

Language-model systems put new pressure on this, because the output isn't a function of the input in the old sense. The same input can produce different outputs. Quality varies by segment. And there's no specification of correct behaviour short of a graded set of examples.

So the acceptance criterion changes form. Instead of one example that must pass, it's a rate on a population that must clear a bar, with an interval around the rate. That's why this chapter leans on the sample-size arithmetic of chapter 11.
a359722d10:
Two statistical ideas keep coming back.

The first is the interval around a proportion. Edwin Wilson's 1927 score interval behaves well at the small samples and high accuracies where evaluation sets live. Every probe in the companion code uses it.

The second is the rule of three (Hanley and Lippman-Hand, 1983). If you see no failures in n trials, the 95 percent upper bound on the failure rate is about 3/n. Fifty-nine clean cases bound the failure rate near 5 percent. Ninety-nine bound it near 3 percent.

These two results turn the sponsor's question, how sure are you, into an arithmetic answer. They're the reason a requirement card carries a sample size next to every bar.
a333ee27a0:
Decisions have a lineage as well. Michael Nygard's 2011 essay on architecture decision records proposed a short, dated, immutable document per significant decision: context, decision, consequences. The records survive because they answer the question every successor asks: why on earth did they do it this way.

Responsibility assignment matrices (the RACI family) have long settled who does, who decides, who is asked and who is told in project management. The stakeholder power-interest grid is usually credited to Aubrey Mendelow (check the original sources if you need to cite it).

Goodhart's law comes from a 1975 observation by the economist Charles Goodhart, phrased in its familiar form by Marilyn Strathern in 1997. When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. It's the single most useful warning for anyone choosing success metrics for an assistant whose usage can be gamed.

Model cards (Mitchell and others, 2019) extended the habit of writing things down to the model itself. Nothing in this chapter is new. The contribution is applying old, well-tested habits to a component whose behaviour is statistical.
a6c9f678bf:
A discovery effort isn't a requirements-gathering marathon. It has a single job. Find the handful of unknowns that, depending on their value, change the architecture. Then replace each guess with a measurement or a named decision.

A language-model solution has about six such unknowns. Know them, and the pattern from chapter 2, the model tier from chapter 4, the guardrails from chapter 13 and the acceptance bars nearly write themselves. Guess them, and you'll rebuild, usually after the demo and before the audit.
6ee5aa83f0:
Notice what's absent from the list: the choice of model, the prompt, the vector store. Those are answers. Discovery produces the questions they answer.

A useful test for any discovery activity is to ask which of the seven unknowns it reduces, and by how much. A stakeholder interview that learns the team's favourite dashboard colour reduces none. Now take a thirty-minute look at last quarter's ticket data. It reveals the baseline handling time is 11 minutes, not 9. That reduces the baseline unknown, and the new number moves the payback by two months (example 04 shows how sensitive payback is).

Spend time on discovery in proportion to the cost of the flip it prevents. The costliest flips are almost always the first, third and fifth rows: the cost of error, the baseline, and who can say no.
6d4f4e355d:
Structure means you decide beforehand who must be heard, what you need from each, in what order, and what you'll do with the answers.

The usual failure goes like this: an interview with the sponsor, a demo of a prototype, and an assumption that the sponsor spoke for everyone. A sponsor knows the goal and the budget. They rarely know the real error cost (the frontline does), the data constraints (the data owner does), the legal limits (privacy counsel does), the attack surface (security does) or the operational reality at peak (operations does).

Six roles cover almost every enterprise assistant. Each owns a distinct slice of the ten question families.
ed2d2b7254:
The order matters too.

  • Interview the frontline before the sponsor if you can. The frontline's description of the error cost is the thing the sponsor will later deny.
  • Interview data and security before design, because their answers close options.
  • Interview legal before anyone has seen a prototype. A prototype creates a commitment, and the legal answer might invalidate it.
  • Interview operations before you set a latency target. The target is only real if someone will carry the pager for it.
2f0a0f6a69:
Read the gap list the way a project manager would.

Five of the nine findings are interviews that never covered a family their role owns. Legal was never asked about compliance or data. Operations was never asked about latency or ops.

Four are segment gaps. Two contract types (MSA and SOW) have a target above the experts' own agreement rate, so no model can be graded as meeting it until the labels are fixed. One type (DPA) has no baseline and no owner, which produces two findings.

The tool also assigns each segment a risk tier from two answers, error impact and reversibility: T1 automated, T2 sampled review, T3 human approves every action. That mapping is deliberately mechanical. It's the same decision as chapter 13's autonomy levels. Making it a function means the sponsor can argue with the inputs, but not with the logic.
9336b5d0c4:
The verbs in a sponsor's first message are improve, reduce, speed up, make accurate, make secure. Each is a direction, and you can't test a direction.

The conversion is the same every time. It has five steps, and each asks one question the sponsor hasn't answered yet.

  • First, what is measured: handling time, wrong credits, escalations. Never quality in the abstract.
  • Second, how much: the threshold, as a number with a unit.
  • Third, against what: the baseline, with a source and a date, so the improvement is a difference and not a feeling.
  • Fourth, for whom: the segment, because an aggregate hides the segment that matters.
  • Fifth, who owns it: the person who can accept a miss. A requirement with no owner has nobody to escalate a failure to.
e710275a11:
The linter is crude on purpose. It catches vague quality words, absolutes (always, never, 100%, zero) and sentences with fewer than two numbers. What it shows is that a rewrite can be checked mechanically.

The rewrite of make it secure and compliant is the instructive one. Security becomes 0 of 500 red-team prompts return an unmasked CPNI field, which you can run before every release. Compliance becomes a retention period and a flagged assumption (confirm with legal). That's honest about what isn't known yet.

Note also what the rewrites don't do. They don't promise zero. Zero wrong credits became no more than 0.5 per 1,000, against a baseline of 1.2. A pilot can actually evidence that target, and the evidence needs a sample size (next section).
f0f8b2033f:
Three habits in the fixed version are worth copying.

  • The out-of-scope line is a requirement. It's the sentence you'll point at when scope grows.
  • Facts nobody has confirmed get placeholders written as confirm with plus a name and a date. The unknown stays visible and owned, not buried in a confident number.
  • Each success line is typed: an outcome (handling time), a guardrail (wrong credits must not get worse) and a leading indicator (acceptance).

Section 14 returns to why all three types are needed.
ddb0acf2ca:
Chapter 1 introduced the requirements card. It's one structured page holding the problem, owner, pillar, baseline, targets by segment, volume, latency, cost ceiling, risk and compliance.

This chapter adds one thing: the card is validated by code before anyone designs against it. A card that passes review by eye can still be wrong. It might have an aggregate bar where a per-segment bar is needed, or an average latency where a percentile is needed. Its evaluation set might be too small to show the bar it claims.

A validator catches those in a second and applies the same rules to every card. It also gives you a place to add a rule the day an incident teaches you a new one.
1582eddc99:
Look at the warning on the good card: unrecognized_charge eval_n 200 allows about 1-2 failures at most before the bar is out of reach. At a 97 percent bar, you need 99 clean cases just to show the bar with no failures. 200 cases leave room for only a few errors.

That warning is the validator telling the architect the evaluation set is too thin for the bar the sponsor liked. It starts one of the most useful conversations the card can start. The sponsor has three choices:

  • accept a lower bar for the first release;
  • fund a larger labelled set;
  • accept a wider interval, and a pilot that reports hold where it would otherwise report go.
bd66cb2f7e:
The arithmetic is short. Suppose a system's true accuracy on a segment were only the bar b. The probability that n independent test cases are all correct is b to the n. To be 95 percent sure the true accuracy is above b after seeing no failures, you need b^n at most 0.05. So n is at least ln(0.05)/ln(b). For b = 0.95 that's 59; for 0.97 it's 99; for 0.99 it's 299.

One failure raises the requirement sharply, to roughly 93 cases at 95 percent. With a failure in hand, you now have to rule out a lower true rate.

So every bar on a card should sit beside the sample that supports it. A bar of 99 percent per segment with 200 cases isn't a stricter requirement than 95 percent with 200 cases. It's an untestable one, and that's exactly why the validator refuses it.
0dd0062b62:
Your day job is Java and Spring, where the same check belongs in a unit test and a startup validation. The port uses records for the card, the same nClean arithmetic, and a list of findings.

In a Spring service, bind the card with @ConfigurationProperties (or load a YAML file in a test). Fail the application context if validate() returns anything. Then a pull request that edits cards/billing-dispute.yaml and drops a bar owner fails CI, and nobody has to remember to look.
f1c346af92:
Before the business case is signed, someone has to answer a plain question. Can a model do this at all, on our data, at roughly the quality the card asks for?

A feasibility probe answers it cheaply. Take a stratified sample of real cases: not the easy ones, and not only the common types. Label them with the experts who will own the bar. Run the candidate model tiers. Report accuracy per segment with an interval.

The purpose isn't to prove the system works. It's to find three groups of segments: the obviously fine, the obviously not, and the ones where you don't know yet. Chapter 11 develops grading and statistics. The point here is how you communicate the result, and how it feeds the decision to proceed.
e67631eabc:
The decision rule in the companion code has three outcomes, and it's stricter than people expect.

  • GO when the lower bound of the 95 percent interval is at or above the bar.
  • NO-GO when the upper bound is below the bar.
  • HOLD otherwise, which means collect more cases.

The point estimate would call a 96 percent observation a pass at any sample size. The interval says that 96 percent on 100 cases is compatible with a true accuracy anywhere from about 90 to 98.4 percent.
7218184b45:
Read the three tables as one story.

At 100 cases per segment, every segment is HOLD. That includes late fees, which are really 99 percent accurate. The sample is simply too small to separate a good segment from a lucky one.

At 400, two segments become GO. Promotions becomes NO-GO: its upper bound, 93.0 percent, is below the 95 percent bar. Installment is still HOLD, with an observed 97.0 percent whose lower bound of 94.8 percent is a hair under the bar.

At 1,000, installment is GO.

So the architect's message to the sponsor is segment-specific and honest: three of four types are on track, promotions needs a different design (a stronger tier or a retrieval fix, chapter 12) before it can be piloted, and I need about 1,000 labelled installment cases to certify it. A single blended 'we are at 96 percent' would have hidden the one segment that decides the project.
35fa1f1378: Sponsors read HOLD as you are not sure. Reframe it as a cost. Another 600 labelled installment cases, at about 30 seconds each, is five hours of expert time. That's cheaper than a launch whose bar can't be defended. And it turns an open question into a scheduled task with an owner.
0fd307eb54:
A feasibility probe says the model can do the work. A business case says the work is worth doing at this cost, against the alternatives, by someone who will be held to the number. They're separate questions, and a sponsor will conflate them. A good demo makes the second feel answered.

The case has to stand on a model of unit economics that anyone in finance can read, with the assumptions labelled and the sensitivities shown. Chapter 1 built the first version of this model for BYOD activation orders. Here the case is the billing-dispute assistant at one region, 38,000 cases per month. And the lesson is a different one: the term that decides the answer is rarely the term the sponsor is looking at.
550456984a:
The model has four lines.

  • Gross saving is volume times adoption times minutes saved times the loaded cost per minute. The assistant only saves time on cases where an agent actually uses the draft.
  • Error cost is volume times the added wrong-output rate times the cost of one wrong output. If the assistant makes errors a human wouldn't have made, they're a cost. A business case that omits them is optimistic by construction.
  • Token cost is volume times the unit cost from your design. Chapter 2's ADR gives $0.0063 per case for the router design.
  • Run cost is the fixed monthly cost of monitoring, evaluation refresh and an on-call share. Most first cases forget it.

Payback is the build cost divided by the monthly net.
d17debe942:
The three scenarios and the break-evens carry the message a finance partner needs.

  • In the expected case, the assistant nets about $32,000 a month and pays back a $320,000 build in 10.0 months.
  • In the pessimistic case (adoption 45 percent, 2.0 minutes saved, added error rate 0.5 points), it loses $11,000 a month and never pays back.
  • In the optimistic case, it pays back in 4.3 months.

The break-even adoption is 30 percent. The break-even cost per wrong credit is $461, against an assumed $180.

Those two numbers are the ones to put in front of the sponsor: the case holds as long as more than three in ten agents use the draft and a wrong credit costs us less than $461. They turn a debate about whether the forecast is right into a check on two measurable quantities during the pilot.
42f63050ec:
A point estimate invites the response but what if it is 14 months? The honest answer is that it very well might be.

So replace each uncertain input with a range (low, most likely, high). Draw many samples, and report the probability of clearing the sponsor's hurdle. The companion example draws 20,000 samples, with triangular distributions for adoption, minutes saved, added error rate, cost per error and build overrun.
d76f2a1c8e:
Three observations are worth stating to a sponsor.

First, the median payback (15 months) is later than the expected-case payback (10 months), because the inputs have long right tails. Adoption can't exceed 100 percent but can sit well below the mode. Error cost can run to twice the estimate.

Second, the inputs that drive the spread are adoption, the added error rate and minutes saved, in that order of rank correlation (about 0.5 each). None of them is a model-cost input.

Third, the correct decision isn't proceed because the expected value is positive. It's proceed to a six-week pilot whose job is to measure adoption and the added error rate, because those two numbers decide whether this is a 10-month or a never case. A pilot is the cheapest way to reduce the variance in the inputs that matter.

Chapter 1's sensitivity example does the same job for one input at a time. The Monte Carlo view adds the joint effect.
17da673e75:
A business case that compares the assistant only with doing nothing flatters it. Put at least two alternatives beside it, with the same arithmetic. One is a non-LLM option: a rules engine for the deterministic eligibility check, or a better template library for the replies. The other is a partial option: the assistant on the two highest-volume types only.

In the dispute example, a rules-based eligibility checker costs less to run and removes most of the wrong credits at the source. Given the waterfall, that may be worth more than the drafting assistant. If so, the right recommendation is to build the checker first and the drafting assistant second, and the case should say so.

CCAR-P rewards exactly this behaviour. The Claude solution is recommended when it wins on the numbers, and not otherwise. Chapter 1's fit test is the first filter; this section is the second.
1f50261cb4: Saving 2.8 minutes on 65 percent of 38,000 cases frees roughly 1,150 hours a month in the region. Whether that becomes lower cost, shorter queues, or growth without hiring is a business decision. The case should name which one the sponsor is committing to. A case that claims cash from released minutes, without naming the decision, gets challenged at the first finance review.
a16e11e3af:
The classical software engineer promises behaviour: given this input, the system returns this output. A language-model system promises a rate. On this kind of input the output meets the rubric this often, and when it doesn't, this happens.

That change of grammar is the hardest communication task in the chapter. Stakeholders carry a lifetime of intuition from deterministic software, where a bug is a defect with a cause and a fix. In a statistical system, a wrong output is an expected event with a known frequency. The engineering response isn't elimination but containment: detect it, route it, bound its cost.

Executives don't need the mathematics. They need three translations.
e3272abd91:
Translate a rate into cases. At 260,000 disputes a month, 95 percent accuracy means 13,000 outputs that need correction, about 433 a day. A 99 percent system means 2,600 a month. In the sponsor's head the percentage feels the same size whether it's 95 or 99. The case count doesn't, and the case count is what lands on someone's desk.

Translate a rate into a probability of at least one. At 99 percent accuracy, a batch of 100 cases contains at least one error 63 percent of the time. A demo of five cases, an acceptance test of ten, and a week of monitoring each see only the part of the rate they're large enough to see.

Translate non-determinism into hard cases, not randomness. A system that gives different answers to the same question isn't 'random' the way a coin is. It has easy cases where it's nearly always right, and a minority of hard cases where it's close to a coin flip. The stakeholder sees that mixture as inconsistency.
cca8be4924:
The formula behind the dashed line is short. Take a case where each run is right with probability p. Two independent runs agree with probability p squared plus (1 minus p) squared. For p = 0.995 that's 99.0 percent; for p = 0.6 it's 52 percent. Average over the mix and you get the curve.

The practical consequences are for design, not only for talk.

  • Don't test a prompt change with one run per case. The run-to-run noise on hard cases swamps small differences (chapter 12).
  • Don't tell an agent that a rerun will give the same answer.
  • Send the hard cases to a human tier, because that's where the variance lives. The model's own confidence and the gates can flag them.
c0ce784660:
The same risk lands differently on four readers, because each owns a different veto.

  • The executive owns the money and the reputation. They decide how much risk the organisation will carry for what return.
  • Legal and privacy own the question of whether the thing is lawful and defensible. They decide whether data may be used at all.
  • Security owns the question of what a hostile party could make the system do. They decide which authority the system may hold.
  • Operations owns the question of who carries the pager and what happens at peak. They decide whether the thing can actually run.

A single deck for all four is read by none of them. The executive skips the data-flow slide. Security skips the payback slide. The question each cared about is answered in an appendix nobody opens.

The discipline is to write the facts once, in one place. Then render a brief per audience. Each brief selects different facts, uses that audience's words, and ends in the one decision or action requested of that reader.
751fdd4f8f:
The test at the bottom of the example is the point of the exercise. Each brief must:

  • contain what its reader needs: payback and a dollar figure for the executive; data classes and retention for legal; a threat and a control for security; a runbook and a kill switch for operations;
  • contain exactly one decision requested;
  • stay under a hundred words;
  • avoid the vocabulary that loses that reader.

The executive version says nothing about tokens or embeddings. It does state the stop rule, because an executive who knows how the pilot can be ended will approve starting it.

The legal version carries a flag, confirm against the retention schedule. The architect doesn't set the retention period and shouldn't look as if they do.

The security version leads with the threat, not the architecture. The reviewer's first question is always what can the attacker make it do.
c77ae6d5be:
A risk register is communication as much as engineering. It's how a legal reviewer finds the row about retention without reading the design. It's how an executive sees that the largest residual risks have an owner and a control.

Chapter 13 develops the FMEA-style scoring: severity, occurrence and detectability, with detectability scored 10 when hard to detect. It also sets the rule that severity at or above 9 needs a deterministic control, no matter how low the product.

The companion generator here applies that machinery to a requirement card. Features of the card switch rules on and off: writes enabled, data classes, untrusted text, regulated decisions, third-party model, volume. Each rule carries defaults, an owner role, an audience and a control.
842d2affde:
Take three things from the output.

First, the draft is fast, and complete enough to review in a workshop. It finds eleven risks for the dispute assistant, and six for a read-only variant with no personal data and no writes. The register shrinks when the card does. That's the argument for narrow authority, in one table.

Second, the top row isn't a model failure. It's reviewer rubber-stamps approvals, a human failure inside the very control the design relies on. That's why the design carries seeded canaries and a minimum review time.

Third, the CPNI row ranks eighth by product, yet carries severity 9. The generator's check enforces that a severity 9 row has a deterministic control (user-scoped tokens, verified recipient). Ranking by product alone would put a regulatory disclosure below an adoption problem. A register is only useful if it contains rules like that, not only scores.
3bfc41ba3a:
Treat the generated register as a starting point to edit, never a deliverable. The owner column is a role from the card; the workshop confirms a named person. The occurrence column is a guess until the pilot, so the register has a re-scoring date.

And every row has an audience. When the register goes out, legal receives the data rows, security the injection rows, and the executive the three rows that could stop the program.
c8b360dcf3:
Stakeholders differ on two axes that matter to a plan: how much they can change the outcome (power), and how much they care about it (interest).

  • A sponsor with both gets a weekly conversation.
  • A high-power, low-interest finance partner gets a short note at each gate and a clean chance to say no.
  • A low-power, high-interest frontline agent gets a representative on the design review and a visible channel for edits. They'll decide whether the thing is used.

The grid is old and simple. What makes it useful here is that each stakeholder also gets a stance and a set of hard demands on named attributes (p95, review share, retention, authority). You can intersect the demands. That turns a vague sense of friction into a list of attributes where no value satisfies everyone.
cca437f359:
The conflict finder reports one attribute with an empty intersection: human review share. AppSec wants at least 20 percent of outputs reviewed. Care team leads want no more than 12 percent, because every review is a minute not spent on the next contact. No design can satisfy both statements as written.

The finder doesn't report the cost-per-case difference between sponsor (at most $0.020) and finance (at most $0.012) as a conflict. $0.012 satisfies both. That's a tighter target, not a collision.

That distinction is the useful thing to teach stakeholders. Most 'conflicts' in a first meeting are different tightness in the same direction. They dissolve into the strictest value, which the architect should adopt unless it's infeasible. A true conflict is an empty intersection, and it needs a different move.
dad81a3c9c: Sometimes the demands don't split. The next tool is to put the design options and the demands in one matrix, and find the options that satisfy every hard limit. If none does, find the one with the smallest violation, and bring that number to the person who owns the limit. Companion example 12 does this with the four designs from chapter 2.
8859c3c592:
When Care Ops tightens p95 to 6 seconds, no option is feasible. The closest is B, with one violation, 28 percent over.

The right message to the decision owner is one question with a number: accept 7.7 seconds, or fund caching and a faster tier and re-run the probe. It isn't a negotiation about whose requirement matters more. It lets the owner trade in the currency they control.

The same technique works when legal and the sponsor disagree on a retention period, or finance and the architect disagree on a build budget. Show the feasible region, show the closest miss, name the owner of the limit.
b8f7edc2cb:
Every stalled AI project has an activity nobody owned. The person who would sign the go-live was never named. The evaluation set had two owners, and each assumed the other would refresh it. The security review sat in someone's inbox, because the request went to a mailing list.

RACI is the cheapest remedy. For each activity, each role is one of four things:

  • Responsible: does the work.
  • Accountable: owns the outcome and can say yes or no. There's exactly one.
  • Consulted: asked before, two-way.
  • Informed: told after, one-way.

The matrix is boring, and it prevents most of the arguments that begin I thought you were doing that. What makes it a design artifact rather than a formality is that you can check it.
f68e5f703e:
Five rules catch nearly all the damage.

  • Exactly one A per activity. Two accountable parties means nobody is.
  • At least one R. Someone must do the work.
  • At most three C. Each consulted party is a wait, and five of them is a committee.
  • No orphan roles. A role that appears nowhere was either not needed or was forgotten.
  • And a rule specific to AI work, separation of duties. Whoever builds the evaluation set must not be the sole signatory on the go/no-go for the same system. It's the same reason the author of a change doesn't approve it.

The example validates a clean matrix and then a damaged one.
690102a38f:
One more habit: put RACI next to the review calendar. Say a security review is 'Consulted' at the tool-gate design. If the request goes in late, that's a week of waiting. If you ignored it until the freeze, it's a two-week wait. The matrix tells you whom to book, and the booking tells you the real go-live date.

On the exam, a launch blocked by an approval nobody planned for is a RACI failure. The correct answer names the role that should have been Accountable, not the one who should work faster.
fe2c46ea21:
A sponsor's idea of success is usually one number. A working system needs a small set:

  • an outcome metric, the thing the business wants (median handling time, wrong credits per 1,000);
  • one or two leading indicators that move earlier and let you steer (draft acceptance rate, edit distance);
  • at least one guardrail that must not get worse while the others improve (audited draft quality, wrong credits).

Each metric needs a definition with a denominator, a baseline, a target, an owner and a cadence.

Leading indicators are valuable and dangerous in equal measure. They move first, which is why you use them. But people can move them without improving the outcome, so they invite Goodhart's law.
02bd810b81:
The scorecard flags the pattern mechanically: acceptance up, audited quality down by more than half a point week over week.

A team that reported only acceptance and handling time would have seen a rising line and a falling minute count. It would have called the pilot a success in week 8, at 88.6 percent audited quality. The guardrail exposes it. And the guardrail must come from an independent sample (the weekly audit of 50 drafts per type), not from the agents' own clicks.

The fix isn't 'trust agents less'. It's designing the incentive so that accepting a bad draft costs something. Show agents their edit-after-send rate. Seed bad drafts to measure the catch rate. Never use acceptance as an individual performance metric.
f72281b5cf:
A pilot is an experiment with a decision attached. A demo is a performance.

People often confuse them, and the confusion is expensive. An impressive demo creates momentum. Momentum creates a commitment. And the commitment is made before the evidence that would justify it exists.

Keep them apart. The demo's job is to make a stakeholder understand what the system does and doesn't do. The pilot's job is to collect the numbers that decide whether to widen it. Every design choice below follows from that split.
73a1375ee4:
Stage one is shadow. The system produces drafts that are logged and never shown. It costs nothing in customer impact, and gives you real-traffic accuracy, latency and cost. The exit rule is agreement with the agent's actual decision on enough cases per segment.

Stage two is assisted. Agents see the draft and decide. This adds adoption, edit rate and the human side of the error rate. The exit rule is every segment GO or EXTEND on the interval rule, with wrong credits not above baseline.

Stage three is bounded action. The system proposes a credit and a person approves, for credits up to the limit. The exit rule is a measured override rate and zero bypasses of the gate.

Authority grows one stage at a time, and each stage has a number that lets it go back.
d0958f58e7:
Show the sponsor the first table. The rare segment sets the calendar. With 10 percent of cases labelled and a 0.4 percent share, the DPA-amendment type would take almost a year to certify (349 days) at three times the clean-sample size. The common types need about a week.

The architect's options are exactly the three printed:

  • pool the rare type with a related one (and report it pooled);
  • raise the labelling fraction for that type (label 100 percent);
  • launch it as human-only until the volume supports a bar.

The second table gives the pilot's verdict in the only honest form. Late fees are GO at the sample the pilot collected, while the other three types remain EXTEND. So the decision is to widen late fees and keep collecting on the rest. A sponsor who wanted 'the pilot result' gets four results.
89b1ead4dc:
A demo is a sample of ten or twenty cases, chosen by the person giving it. Two statistical facts make it uninformative.

The first is that a flawless run is unlikely even for a good system, which is why people are tempted to pick cases. With 97.1 percent overall accuracy, a ten-case demo is flawless 75 percent of the time, and a twenty-case demo only 56 percent. If the demo contains only the weakest segment (promotions, 91.5 percent), twenty cases are flawless 17 percent of the time.

The second fact is worse. If you rehearse and keep the set that works, a flawless demo becomes almost certain (98 percent with three candidate sets).

So a flawless rehearsed demo carries almost no information about the system. Yet an audience that has seen one forms a belief about accuracy that the data doesn't support.
910d730c38:
The design rules that follow are simple. The demo-script linter in the example enforces four of them.

  • Show a failure on purpose: a case where the system abstains or escalates, so the audience sees the safety path work.
  • Show the numbers: one slide with per-segment results and sample sizes, including the worst segment.
  • Show at least three segments, one of them the hardest.
  • Show what it will not do: the out-of-scope list from the card, read aloud.

Add one more for the audience. Let a stakeholder choose a case from the real queue, unseen, and run it live. How the system behaves on a case it wasn't rehearsed on is the most honest thing you can show.
0a69dcc938:
An architect who can't say no is a bottleneck dressed as a partner. The skill is saying it so the requester is better off than when they asked.

There are four distinct no's, and mixing them up is the common mistake.

  • Redirect means another tool is better. The problem is deterministic, so code is cheaper, faster and exactly repeatable (chapter 1's fit test).
  • Decline means the request as stated can't be met or doesn't pay. It asks for 100 percent, or its payback exceeds the policy.
  • Not yet means prerequisites are missing: no owner, no approved source content, no data.
  • Yes with conditions accepts the work with constraints that follow from the risk: human approval for every action, per-segment bars, a shadow stage first.

Every one of them carries a sentence of the form here is what would change the answer.
0354187c5d:
Decisions that live in a meeting evaporate in a quarter. The person who made them moves teams. The slide deck gets edited. The reasoning is reconstructed as a story that fits the current design.

The remedy is a short, dated, owned record per significant decision, stored with the code or the card. Chapter 2 gave an ADR for the pattern choice. This chapter adds the stakeholder side. The same record states who was consulted, who owned the decision, what wasn't decided, and what measurable change reopens it.

The template adds three fields that general-purpose ADRs often omit: evidence (the evaluation run behind the numbers), the unit cost, and the review triggers.
c8b13904b4:
A template isn't enough, because teams fill templates with 'Agent. Best.' The linter checks the habits that make an ADR useful:

  • status and owner exist;
  • the context cites a requirements-card version, so the numbers have a referent;
  • there are at least three options, and each has at least two numbers;
  • every rejected option names the requirement it violates;
  • the consequences include something negative;
  • there are at least two review triggers, and each is measurable;
  • a not decided here section exists, to keep the decision from growing into things it never covered.

The Java port carries the same rules, for a CI step that fails the build on a missing field.
3816ac74e8:
Notice what the bad ADR is missing. It isn't eloquence. It's six structural things a reviewer would want within thirty seconds.

That's the reason to lint. A review comment that says 'add the numbers' is a conversation. A failing check that says 'option without numbers: A. Agent. Best.' is a fact, and a team that sees it twice stops writing them.

Two conventions help ADRs stay alive. First, they're immutable once accepted. A change is a new ADR that supersedes the old one, and the old one's status changes to Superseded. That preserves the history of why the first decision was reasonable at the time. Second, they're linked to the artefacts they govern: the card version, the evaluation set, the pipeline config. A future reader can then reproduce the evidence.
ec18030054:
Two habits keep discovery from leaking.

The first is to read meeting notes the way an auditor reads a contract: for promises. A stakeholder says it always has to follow policy. The architect nods. Six weeks later that sentence is quoted back as a requirement.

The linter in example 18 finds three kinds of problem in notes:

  • absolutes spoken by a stakeholder (100 percent, always, never, zero);
  • actions without an owner or date (we should look at the escalation volumes sometime);
  • numbers without a source (we assume 70 percent adoption, it is what the vendor said).

For each finding it drafts the follow-up question. The regular expressions are crude. The point is the discipline. Every absolute gets restated as a rate with a sample size. Every action gets a name and a date. Every number gets a source, or a label that says it's an assumption.
6a927897b2:
Notice what the linter deliberately doesn't flag. The architect's own sentence, I can't promise 100%, contains an absolute. But it's a refusal to commit, not a commitment. The rule targets promises made to us and by us in an unmeasured way.

A real implementation would use a model to find commitments in free-form notes, with the same discipline as the next example: the model proposes and the code verifies.
321e7209ce:
Interview notes are exactly the kind of input where a model saves time. They're also exactly where it can invent a number.

The pattern that holds up is a forced tool call whose schema requires a verbatim quote next to every fact. A code check then confirms the quote appears in the source. Facts whose quotes don't verify never reach the card. They go back to the interviewee for confirmation.

The scripted model in the example returns five facts: three correct and two defective. One quote paraphrases a number the notes state differently (twelve minutes where the notes say nine). The other drops the word never and inverts the fact about the weekend queue. The verifier rejects both.
a2ab1163e3:
Three details deserve attention.

First, tool_choice forces the named tool, so the response is structured, not prose. (See chapter 4 for the tool-choice options, and check the docs for the current parameter names.)

Second, the system prompt says what the model must not do (infer). But the verifier doesn't rely on that instruction. A prompt is a request; the quote check is a control.

Third, the check is a plain substring test after whitespace normalisation. It's strict by design, because a paraphrase that changes a number or drops a negation is exactly the failure it exists to catch. The strictness costs a few false rejections that a person resolves in seconds. In return, nothing a model invented can reach the requirements card.

It's the same fail-closed stance the rest of CCAR-P takes toward model output (chapters 2 and 13), applied to the discovery process itself.
1611e537e8:
Expectations set at the start decay. Volume grows. A model snapshot changes. A new product launches. The agents who loved the pilot are replaced. Slowly, the expectations contract of section 09 stops describing the system.

A feedback loop is the mechanism that keeps what stakeholders believe aligned with what the system does. It has four parts:

  • a signal: what is measured, and by whom;
  • a cadence: how often it's reviewed;
  • a threshold: the value at which someone must act;
  • an owner: who acts.

Chapter 16 develops the SLA, lifecycle and handoff documents in full. The point here is the shape of the communication that rides on them.
1e4f395f6b:
The table is a communication plan as much as a monitoring plan. The last column says who learns what. That's what keeps privacy counsel from reading about a gate bypass in a quarterly review.

Pair it with a standing artefact per audience: a one-page monthly note to the sponsor, a quarterly review of the register for legal and security, a weekly dashboard for operations. Then expectation maintenance is a habit, not a reaction to a bad week.

One principle ties the loops to the earlier sections: change the expectation before the system changes it for you. Say hard cases are rising, and the escalation rate will go from 12 to 18 percent. Tell operations and the sponsor first, with the reason and the effect on the savings. Don't let the dashboard do it for you.
845a177f7e:
Run the check weekly and let it generate the first line of the sponsor's note. Where drift is favourable (p95 better than promised), say so. Where it's unfavourable, say what you'll do.

Comparing the contract with the observation is what turns the contract into a living document. And a stakeholder who sees the architect volunteer the bad news before the dashboard does extends more trust at the next review.
f30960f91a:
The fixed update gives the same good news, and adds the one number that changes the plan. It's also easier to write once the card and the scorecard exist, because the structure is the same each week: outcome, leading, guardrail, cause, action, owner, decision requested.

The skill isn't honesty as a virtue. It's that an update with a guardrail line makes the sponsor an ally in the stop rule before the stop rule is needed.
2db4b67c49: CCAR-P scenarios in this domain have four plausible answers. The winning one usually makes the requirement testable, brings the right person in at the right time, and states a trade-off with evidence. Work each scenario before reading the reasoning.
